paragraphs.text: Why 1 broken cable cut off Tonga.

The eruption on 14 January 2022 sent an ash column 58 km high and caused faults in the international cable 37 km from Nukuʻalofa and a domestic cable 47 km away, breaking the Tonga Cable System that connects the nation to Southern Cross’s trans‑Pacific line in Fiji. Tonga’s international internet relied on that single submarine link, and a repair vessel arrived on 30 January.

Cable landing points are uncommon and often serve as the shared shore entry for multiple systems. Sometimes the cable runs miles inland before reaching a termination facility, which may be a landing station or a separate termination station depending on power needs. Repeaters can require voltages of 3 000–4 000 V for trans‑Atlantic telecom cables or 1 000 V for cross‑channel links.

Termination stations can coincide with landing stations or be far from the coast, as the Endeavour system linking Australia to Hawaii shows, and the Sydney landing at Tamarama Beach lies four kilometres from the Paddington termination point. For power cables the termination may be the first land‑based cable sleeve or a distant HVDC inverter plant.

A cable landing point commonly denotes where submarine telecom or power cables reach land. Landings may occur directly for point‑to‑point systems or through a branch off a main cable employing a submarine branching unit. Such a branch may extend for multiple kilometres.
The cable lands on shore and links the islands to the global network; repairs need a specialist ship.
Tonga depended on a single international submarine cable, providing no alternative path for data traffic.
The volcanic eruption severed the submarine cable, leaving Tonga without international connectivity until repair crews can restore service.
A cable landing point refers to the spot where an undersea communications cable reaches the shore.
Satellite links restored limited service in the meantime.

miniNarrative: Southern Cross Cable reported that the eruption may have broken the Tonga Cable System, which connects Tonga to Southern Cross's trans-Pacific cable in Fiji.
Southern Cross cited a fault in the international cable 37 km (23 mi) from Nukuʻalofa, and a further fault in a domestic cable 47 km (29 mi) from Nukuʻalofa.
A large eruption commenced on 14 January 2022 at 04:20 local time, sending clouds of ash 20 km into the atmosphere.
The eruption column from this eruption rose 58 km (36 mi) into the mesosphere.
